name: Transpiration bag
summary: A clear bag tied over a leafy living branch collects the water the tree is already pumping — far more yield than a solar still, for far less work.
time: set at dawn, collect at dusk

materials.item: a leafy branch of a non-toxic tree

steps.text: Pick a healthy, leafy, sun-exposed branch of a tree you have positively identified as non-toxic.
Slip the bag over as much foliage as it will hold and tie the mouth tight around the branch.
Put a small stone in one low corner and arrange the bag so that corner is the lowest point.
steps.why: Condensate has to run somewhere. Without a deliberate low corner it beads on the whole surface and drips back onto the leaves.

steps.text: Leave it through the hot part of the day and drain the corner in the evening.
Move the bag to a fresh branch each day.

verify: Water is pooling in the low corner by mid-afternoon. Nothing by then means too little sun, too few leaves, or a leaking tie.
limits: The yield is water the plant transpired — typically a few hundred millilitres per bag per day, and less in dry or cool conditions. It is a supplement, not a supply.
It cannot work at night, in shade, or on a dormant plant.
The water is distilled but not sterile: it picks up whatever is on the leaves and inside the bag.
cautions: Never bag a toxic species — oleander, yew, poison ivy/oak/sumac and their relatives put their toxin into the condensate. If you cannot identify the tree, do not use it.
A solar ground still is the famous alternative and is usually a net LOSS: in most conditions you sweat out more digging it than it returns.
